awd_titl_txt: Conference: 2025 Midwest Several Complex Variables Conference
awd_abstract_narration:
This award supports participants in the Midwest Several Complex Variables Conference to be held at Texas A&M University during May 16-18, 2025. The Midwest Several Complex Variables Conference series is one of the most important venues for researchers in the field of several complex variables and has influenced generations of researchers at all career stages.  This year’s conference will be held for the first time at Texas A&M University and will provide an excellent opportunity for graduate students and early-career researchers to learn about the latest techniques and trends in several complex variables.  The conference program includes lectures by leading researchers as well as early-career mathematicians, a poster session for graduate students, and an open problem session for conference participants.  More information can be found at https://sites.google.com/view/mwscv2025/home.

The Midwest Several Complex Variables Conference at Texas A&M University will showcase recent developments in several complex variables, functional analysis, operator theory, complex geometry, and related fields. The main topics of this year’s meeting include the Cauchy-Riemann operator, the complex Laplacian, and their applications; the Kohn Laplacian and CR geometry; reproducing kernels and invariant metrics; function theory in several complex variables; and the interplay between several complex variables and operator theory.  These areas have witnessed significant progress in recent years.  The conference will bring together leading experts, early-career researchers, and graduate students in several complex variables and related fields to discuss these recent developments and explore new research frontiers.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
The conference highlighted recent advances in several complex variables and related fields, including CR geometry, the d-bar-Neumann problem, Bergman and Hardy spaces, complex geometry, functional analysis, operator theory, and partial differential equations. The scientific program consisted of 16 research presentations -- seven 50-minute invited lectures and nine 25-minute lectures -- as well as a poster session featuring seven posters by graduate students and early-career researchers. The conference brought together 76 participants, including leading experts, junior faculty, postdoctoral researchers, graduate students, and undergraduate students.

The conference facilitated the exchange of new techniques and ideas, strengthened connections among researchers working in related areas, and provided opportunities to initiate new collaborations and research projects. The conference was especially beneficial to early-career participants, including 16 graduate students, five undergraduate students, 12 postdoctoral researchers, and seven assistant professors. Junior researchers had opportunities to present their work, receive feedback from established experts, learn about emerging research directions, and develop professional connections. These activities contributed to their research training, professional development, and future career prospects.

NSF funding covered travel and lodging expenses for invited speakers, graduate students, and early-career researchers, making broad participation possible. The organizers also contacted universities throughout the Midwest and South to encourage participation and to strengthen the regional research community in several complex variables and related fields.
